newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialists face job challenge in car sector.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists face job challenge in car sector.

text.p: The French car industry's plan to slim down and shed jobs could set it on a collision course with the new Socialist-led government, which campaigned on a promise to bring down France's record 12.8 percent unemployment rate.
The Socialist leaders had only just taken office this week when the motor industry announced fresh staff cuts.
Automobiles Peugeot, the car division of PSA Peugeot Citroen sprang the announcement on Tuesday that it would cut 2,816 jobs, around five percent of its staff.
The news came just as the new Socialist-led government was gearing up to tackle Renault's socially explosive decision to shut down its Vilvoorde plant in Belgium.

Industry analysts said the Socialists would probably accept that some restructuring of France's fragmented and high-cost car industry is needed but they were still likely to delay the process and add to the cost.
From their earliest pronouncements, the Socialist leaders have been pushing Renault to consider alternatives to closing the Vilvoorde plant, which employs about 3,000 people.
"We saw a brutal decision come down and, in our opinion, all the possibilities had not been explored," Elisabeth Guigou, the new justice minister, said this week.
Renault reiterated this week that the plant shutdown was essential. It is also cutting 2,800 jobs in France this year and expects similar job cuts in each of the next few years.

The lossmaking company's troubles did not come up at the first cabinet meeting of the new government on Thursday. "We did not discuss that issue today. It will be taken up by the minister concerned and obviously by the prime minister," a government spokeswoman said.
Finance and Industry Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn is viewed by the financial markets as "one of the safe hands in the Socialist Party", according to one investment firm economist.

"I don't think the government will make them go back on their plans, but it can't lose face either," said a Paris-based stock analyst. "It may freeze the situation (in Vilvoorde) at least until a buyer is found."

Renault was partly privatised in two stages in 1994 and 1996, but the state remains its biggest shareholder with a 46 percent stake and has five directors on the 15-member board. Allied with the staff's three representatives, they form a majority.
Share prices in Renault and the Peugeot group have slipped recently on fears that a Socialist-led government would frown on their restructuring, which analysts say is long overdue.
"I suspect we'll hear noise about how terrible these restructurings are, but they can't make it impossible for these companies to press on," said John Lawson at Salomon Brothers.

"At the end of the day, the Socialists face the same issue as the centre-right, which is that there is a crisis in the French car industry. Come August, both companies will be reporting first-half losses, while in the rest of Europe many car companies will be reporting better figures," he said.

Lawson said fiscal incentives to boost demand, such as the new-cars-for-old rebates put in place by the past two conservative governments, were no substitute for restructuring and had "nearly mollycoddled the industry to death".

France's car companies, the smallest of the six full-range manufacturers in Europe, are struggling. They are overly dependent on the slow-growing European market, and their home market is weak. French car sales fell nearly 23 percent in the first four months of the year over the same period in 1996.
The European industry is saddled with overcapacity which has fuelled a price war that has been particularly savage in France.
Renault estimates its share of the industry's overcapacity at 200,000 cars per day, the equivalent of one plant's output.
But trade unions, heartened by the Socialist election victory, want the government to push the car companies into reducing working hours to spread the available work around.

"They ask people to work overtime, they want them to work Saturdays, they take away their weekends, and they refuse any negotiations on reducing work-weeks. It's scandalous," said a spokesman for the Communist CGT union, the largest at Renault.
